title: Efficient multicolor X-ray excited persistent luminescence enabled by Gd-mediated trap clusters

paper_content.abstract: Persistent luminescence materials are promising for night-vision displays, background-free medical diagnostics, and high-resolution radiography, yet achieving efficient violet, yellow, and red emission within a single robust and scalable host remains a longstanding challenging. Here, we overcame this limitation by constructing Gd3+-mediated cluster traps within alkaline-earth fluorochlorides to minimize energy loss during electron migration. These clusters serve as both intrinsic emitters and efficient energy transfer platforms for various activators, including Eu2+, Sm2+, Tb3+, and Mn2+, enabling bright and spectrally tunable multicolor persistent luminescence upon X-ray irradiation. The persistent luminescence intensity of Eu2+ is enhanced by up to 32.7-fold upon Gd3+ codoping. Moreover, violet persistent luminescence from Eu2+ is employed to excite perovskite quantum dots for full-color time-domain dynamic displays, while Sm2+ emission facilitates low-dose, high-resolution delayed X-ray imaging. These findings establish a generalizable strategy for designing efficient multicolor persistent materials for advanced multi-functional optical technologies.
paper_content.introduction:
Persistent luminescence (PersL) is a fascinating optical phenomenon wherein materials continue to emit photons following the cessation of excitation1–4. This time-delayed photon emission holds great promise for a wide range of applications, including optical data storage5–7, night-vision displays8, background-free medical diagnostics9 and high-resolution radiography10,11. Despite being discovered in the early 17th century, efficient inorganic PersL materials remain largely confined to blue-(e.g., CaAl2O4:Eu/Nd)12,13 and green-emitting (e.g., SrAl2O4:Eu/Dy and Sr2MgSi2O7:Eu/Dy)14,15 systems. Longer-wavelength emissions, such as yellow and red, are typically achieved in sulfide-based materials16,17, which suffer from poor stability and low brightness, while efficient violet PersL yet to be demonstrated. Extending PersL into the violet, yellow, and red spectral regions with high efficiency, especially using environmentally robust and scalable hosts remains a formidable challenge, hindering progress toward full-color displays18–20, multiplexed bioimaging21, and multichannel information encryption22–24. More critically, realizing multicolor PersL within a single host is exceptionally difficult, yet essential for minimizing compatibility issues and simplifying integration into multi-functional optical devices.

Room-temperature PersL typically arises from the spontaneous release of charge carriers trapped in shallow energy states, followed by their migration through the host lattice and subsequent radiative recombination at luminescent centers25. However, long-range carrier migration is often accompanied by substantial non-radiative losses, including multi-phonon relaxation26, defect-induced quenching27, and inefficient energy transfer28,29, which significantly compromises overall luminescence efficiency. In upconversion luminescence, spatially confining sensitizers and activators into clusters has proven effective for suppressing energy loss by shortening energy transfer distances30. Drawing inspiration from this strategy, we propose that co-localizing traps and activators into confined clusters can significantly enhance PersL by minimizing migration-associated energy dissipation, which in turn provides a powerful approach to realize bright multicolor PersL within a single host lattice through doping with various activators.

As a proof-of-concept, we introduce a Gd3+-mediated cluster engineering strategy in alkaline-earth fluorochloride hosts to confine trap carrier migration (Fig. 1). Substituting divalent alkaline-earth with trivalent Gd3+ induces the formation of [Gd-F-]n clusters. Upon X-ray irradiation, fluoride ions coordinated to Gd3+ preferentially form Frenkel defects, resulting in Gd3+-associated trap clusters that produce intense PersL from Gd3+ itself. More importantly, these clusters serve as efficient energy transfer platforms to various activators, including Eu2+, Sm2+, Tb3+, and Mn2+, enabling bright and spectrally tunable multicolor PersL. Notably, emissions from Eu2+ and Sm2+, despite their narrower full widths at half maximum (FWHM), exhibit much higher brightness than the benchmark green-emitting SrAl2O4:Eu/Dy. Moreover, these fluorochloride-based systems demonstrate superior air stability compared to commercial aluminates. We also demonstrate that the violet PersL from Eu2+ can serve as an excitation source for perovskite quantum dots, enabling full-color dynamic displays. Meanwhile, the red PersL from Sm2+ facilitates low-dose, high-resolution delayed X-ray imaging.
paper_content.results:
Characterization and benchmarking of lanthanide-doped BaFCl phosphors
Lanthanide-doped BaFCl phosphors were scalable synthesized via a conventional scalable solid-state reaction, but under significantly milder conditions (1073 K for 1 h, Supplementary Fig. 1) compared to those typically required for commercial SrAl2O4:Eu/Dy (>1573 K for over 4 h)31. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the products with and without Gd3+ doping matched well with the phase-pure tetragonal BaFCl structure (Supplementary Fig. 2), featuring an optical band gap of 5.73 eV (Supplementary Fig. 3). Atomic-resolution integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM, Fig. 2a) and high-resolution TEM (Supplementary Fig. 4) revealed a highly crystalline microstructure. Elemental mapping (Fig. 2b) and energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. 5) demonstrated the presence of F, Cl, Ba, Gd and Eu elements. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) further confirmed the Eu and Gd doping levels in BaFCl:2Eu/1Gd to be ~1.51 and 0.62 mol%, respectively, closely agreement with the nominal composition. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) of the Eu 3d states revealed the coexistence of Eu2+ (1125, 1155 eV) and Eu3+ (1135, 1165 eV)32, with the Eu3+/Eu2+ ratio remaining unaffected by Gd3+ codoping (Supplementary Fig. 6).

Upon cessation of X-ray irradiation, the BaFCl:Eu exhibited weak PersL, featuring a sharp peak at 365 nm (Eu2+: 6P7/2 → 8S7/2) and a broad emission centered at 387 nm (Eu2+: 4f65d1 → 8S7/2) (Supplementary Fig. 7)33,34. The optimal Eu doping concentration was determined to be ~2 mol% (Fig. S7b, c). Notably, characteristic Eu3+ emission was absent, likely due to its extremely low probability of capturing trapped carriers10. As shown in Fig. 2c, the PersL intensity of BaFCl:Eu is markedly enhanced upon Gd3+ codoping. At an optimal Gd3+ concentration of 1 mol%, the integrated PersL intensity increases by up to 32.7-fold. The PersL decay curves reveal that both the peak intensity and afterglow duration are substantially improved with Gd3+ incorporation (Fig. 2d). The BaFCl:Eu/Gd exhibits rapid charging kinetics, reaching saturation within ~30 s, and maintains detectable PersL for over 100 h at room temperature (Supplementary Fig. 8). Time-lapse photographic images further corroborate the enhanced and long-lasting brightness across various decay intervals (Fig. 2i). Elevating the X-ray tube voltage from 10 to 50 KV resulted in an additional 65.8-fold enhancement in PersL intensity (Fig. 2e), attributed to the increased secondary electron generation and more efficient trap filling at higher excitation energies.

To benchmark performance, we compared the BaFCl:Gd/Eu with several commercial persistent phosphors, including CaAl2O4:Eu/Nd, SrAl2O4:Eu/Dy, Sr13Al22Si10O66:Eu, ZnS:Cu/Co, and CaS:Eu. Remarkably, the BaFCl:Gd/Eu outperformed all references (Fig. 2f), exhibiting significantly stronger PersL across a wider range of X-ray tube voltages (Supplementary Fig. 9). Notably, it shows a much narrower FWHM (~30 nm) compared to 72 nm for SrAl2O4:Eu/Dy, while its integrated PersL intensity is ~3.5 times higher under identical conditions (Supplementary Fig. 10). More importantly, the PersL intensity of BaFCl:Gd/Eu decreased by only ~5% after 60 days of air exposure with repeated irradiation and daily measurements, markedly outperforming SrAl2O4:Eu/Dy and ZnS:Cu/Co (Fig. 2h, and Supplementary Fig. 11), highlighting its superior long-term durability. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 12, the PersL intensity and spectral profile remained nearly unchanged during 60 continuous irradiation cycles (1 min each), confirming that the decrease in PersL intensity of SrAl2O4:Eu/Dy is not associated with X-ray irradiation damage. Despite the extremely low sensitivity of the human eye to violet light, the violet PersL luminance from BaFCl:Gd/Eu still reaches about 0.16 cd m−2 at 2 s after ceasing X-ray irradiation. This outstanding performance is attributed to the high X-ray absorption coefficient and the effective trapping of charge carriers (Supplementary Fig. 13). Additionally, the BaFCl:Gd/Eu achieves a photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) of 92.7%, far exceeding that of SrAl2O4:Eu/Dy (54.7%) (Supplementary Fig. 14). It should be noted that the comparison of reported quantum yields may be affected by the fact that SrAl2O4:Eu/Dy exhibits trapping and detrapping under UV excitation, which can reduce the overall efficiency, whereas BaFCl:Eu does not.

Mechanistic investigations
To uncover the origin of the enhanced PersL, we investigated how heterovalent Gd3+ doping modifies the local structure, trap states, and energy migration dynamics. Extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectroscopy was employed to probe the coordination environment of Gd3+ in the BaFCl lattice. As shown in Fig. 3a, Supplementary Fig. 15, EXAFS fitting reveals that Gd3+ is coordinated by an average of ~2.1 F− and 2.1 Cl− ions, notably lower than the corresponding values for native Ba2+ sites (4.2 for F− and 5.1 for Cl−, Fig. 3b). In addition, the Gd–F bond length is ~1.88 Å, much shorter than the Ba–F bond length of 2.54 Å (Supplementary Table 1), indicating evident local lattice contraction surrounding the Gd3+ dopants. Despite the Gd3+ doping level being below 1 mol%, a distinct Gd–Gd scattering signal is observed in the Fourier-transformed EXAFS spectrum (Fig. 3c). This unexpected signal, combined with the reduced coordination numbers and shortened bond lengths, manifesting the formation of locally aggregated [Gd-F-]n clusters35. In addition, Raman spectroscopic confirms the appearance of an additional Gd–F vibrational mode36,37, in addition to the characteristic phonon modes of the BaFCl host lattice (Supplementary Fig. 16).

To further elucidate the structure of the clusters, density functional theory (DFT) simulations were performed to model the Gd L-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectra for different Gd3+ substitution scenarios. Among the constructed crystal models, the configuration in which six Gd3+ ions replace nine Ba2+ ions and create three Ba2+ vacancies to maintain charge neutrality, produced a calculated XANES spectrum that closely matches the experimental data (Supplementary Fig. 17a, d). In contrast, models with either a single Gd3+ substituting one Ba2+, or two Gd3+ ions replacing three Ba2+ ions yielded simulated XANES profiles that deviate significantly from the experimental spectrum (Supplementary Fig. 17b, c, e, f). These results indicate a strong tendency for Gd3+ ions to aggregate within the BaFCl lattice, forming Gd-rich clusters.

Upon X-ray irradiation, high-energy photons interact with heavy atoms primarily through the photoelectric effect, generating hot electrons and deep holes38. These primary carriers undergo multiple scattering and Auger processes, producing abundant low-energy secondary electrons. Concurrently, the F− related Frenkel defects are formed, acting as carrier traps and generating PersL after the cessation of X-rays39–43. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 18, the current gradually increases upon X-ray irradiation and decays slowly with a delay exceeding 7 s after the X-ray is turned off, while the peak current rises at higher tube voltages. These observations indicate that the measured conductivity predominantly arises from defect-related ionic transport under X-ray irradiation. DFT calculations reveal the formation energy (Ef) of F− Frenkel defects within the [Gd-F-]n clusters, is substantially lower than that of F− bound to Ba2+, indicating the traps preferentially form within the clusters (Fig. 3d). Especially, for surface F− ions within the clusters, the Ef for displacement toward the cluster is significantly lower than that for displacement away from the cluster. In this scenario, both the trapped carriers and the associated recombination energy remains spatially confined within the clusters. To probe the role of Ln3+ doping on trap states while avoiding interference from Gd3+-mediated energy transfer, the optically inert Lu3+ ion with an ionic radius similar to that of Gd3+ was employed as a control dopant. X-ray active thermoluminescence (TL) analysis reveals that Lu3+ doping results in similar shallow traps, with no significant changes in trap depth (~0.76 eV) or density (Supplementary Fig. 19)44. In contrast, codoping with Gd3+ leads to a substantial enhancement in TL intensity below 400 K (Fig. 3e, and Supplementary Fig. 20), which is attributed to efficient charge transfer from the trapped carriers to Gd3+ ions within the clusters, followed by subsequent transfer to Eu2+.

Unlike X-ray excited PersL, which arises from the thermal release and migration of trapped electrons, X-ray excited optical luminescence (XEOL) originates from the recombination of free-electrons in the conduction-band with holes45. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 21, in the absence of Eu2+, strong characteristic Gd3+: (6P5/2 → 8S7/2 at 311 nm and 6P7/2 → 8S7/2 at 316 nm) emissions are observed in the XEOL spectrum46. With increasing temperature or excitation power, the I316nm/I311nm intensity ratio increases, indicating enhanced electron–phonon coupling and elevated nonradiative relaxation via the 6P5/2 → 6P7/2 transition (Supplementary Fig. 22). Upon Eu2+ codoping, the XEOL intensity of Gd3+ is nearly fully quenched (Supplementary Fig. 23), suggesting a near-unity energy transfer efficiency from Gd3+ to Eu2+ (Supplementary Fig. 24). A similar suppression is observed in the PersL intensity (Fig. 3f, and Supplementary Fig. 25) and decay curves (Supplementary Fig. 26) of Gd3+, further supporting this efficient energy transfer pathway. This efficiency arises from both the mean Gd–Eu distance of ~0.81 nm (Supplementary Fig. 27a, b), which is far below the typical critical distance of 2 to 6 nm for Förster resonance energy transfer47,48, and the strong overlap between the Eu3+ excitation spectrum and the Gd3+ emissions spectrum (Supplementary Fig. 27c). Notably, the PersL from Gd3+ in BaFCl:Gd lasts for more than 168 h (Supplementary Fig. 28). However, the XEOL intensity and pulsed X-ray excited life-time of Eu2+ in the BaFCl:Eu/Gd are similar to those in BaFCl:Eu and BaFCl:Eu/Lu (Supplementary Fig. 29), indicating that Gd3+ codoping does not enhance the excitation efficiency of the Eu2+: 5d states via free-electron recombination. This behavior is consistent with the spectral overlap between the broad Eu2+ excitation band and the Gd3+ emission region, where Gd3+ acts as an alternate excitation route rather than enhancing the excitation probability. This interpretation is further supported by the comparable photoluminescence intensity of Eu2+ under various UV excitation wavelengths, irrespective of Gd3+ codoping (Supplementary Fig. 30). These results reveal that if trapped electrons are thermally released as free-electrons before captured by activators, Gd3+ exerts minimal influence on the PersL intensity of Eu2+. Therefore, the observed enhancement in PersL upon Gd3+ doping is attributed to the formation of Gd3+-mediated trap clusters, which localize the trapped electrons and enable their efficient transfer to nearby Eu2+ ions. Monte Carlos simulations30 further reveal that spatial clustering of traps and activators within the lattice significantly increases the activation probability of luminescent centers compared to random distribution (Fig. 3g, h), confirming that energy clustering effectively minimizes energy loss during long-range carrier migration.

Universal enhancement of PersL across diverse activators and hosts
To validate the universality of the Gd3+-mediated trap cluster enhancement mechanism and expand its applicability to multi-color PersL, we investigated additional activators, including divalent Sm2+, trivalent Tb3+ and transition metal Mn2+, as well as alternative fluorochloride hosts such as CaFCl and SrFCl. As shown in Fig. 4a–e and Supplementary Fig. 31, all three dopant systems in the BaFCl host exhibited pronounced increases in PersL intensity upon Gd3+ codoping. The enhancements reach up to 150.3-fold for Sm2+, 22.9-fold for Tb3+, and 20.2-fold for Mn2+ (Fig. 4f), attributed to efficient cascade energy transfer from the trap cluster to Gd3+, and subsequently to the activator (Supplementary Fig. 32). The corresponding decay profiles further confirm that Gd3+ incorporation significantly improves both the PersL intensity and duration (Fig. 4g–i). Time-lapse photographic images intuitively demonstrate enhanced brightness across various decay intervals (Fig. 4j–l). In particular, in the absence of Gd3+, the PresL from Sm2+ and Mn2+ was invisible to the naked eye within 1 s post irradiation, but display clear visible emission even after 60 s with Gd3+ codoping. The initial PersL luminance values of the Sm2+, Tb3+, and Mn2+-doped systems reached 3.28, 0.87, and 0.56 cd m−2, respectively. The BaFCl:Gd/Sm achieves a high PLQY of 84.2% (Supplementary Fig. 33), and its integrated red PresL intensity was ~2.2 times higher than that of green SrAl2O4:Eu/Dy and ~47.8 times greater than that of red CaS:Eu (Supplementary Fig. 34). Furthermore, the Gd3+ codoping strategy was extended to other hosts, including CaFCl:Eu and SrFCl:Eu, yielding enhancements in PersL intensity by 101.5 and 107.8 times, respectively (Fig. 4d–f). These results highlight the broad compatibility of the Gd3+-mediated trap cluster engineering approach across different activator ions and host lattices. Notably, the XEOL intensity of these systems does not increase upon Gd3+ codoping (Supplementary Fig. 35), further confirming that the enhanced PersL originates from the formation of Gd3+-mediated trap clusters.

Full color PersL dynamic displays and low-dose delayed X-ray imaging
The superior violet-range PersL performance of BaFCl:Eu/Gd enables its use as an excitation source for halide perovskite (CsPbX3, X=Cl, Br, I) quantum dots (QDs) (Supplementary Fig. 36), thereby achieving full-spectrum PersL across the visible range. The bandgap and corresponding emission wavelength of the QDs were tuned by varying the halide composition49. A flexible BaFCl:Eu/Gd-integrated flexible PDMS film was placed above dispersions of different QDs, irradiated with X-rays for 30 s, and the resulting PersL photographs were captured using a smartphone after the cessation of X-rays (Supplementary Fig. 37). As shown in Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 38, varying the QD composition from CsPbCl2Br1 to CsPbBr3 and CsPbI3 shifts the persistent emission peaks from 433 to 508 and 686 nm, respectively, covering a continuous color range from blue through green to red. Notably, the QD dispersions alone exhibited no observable XEOL or PersL under X-ray excitation (Supplementary Fig. 39), indicating the full-color PersL arises from radiative energy transfer from the BaFCl:Eu/Gd PersL to the QDs via reabsorption50. To further demonstrate dynamic time-domain multicolor display capability, we designed a composite pattern consisting of BaFCl doped with Eu/Gd, Sm/Gd, and Mn/Gd, along with four selected QDs (CsPbCl2Br1, CsPbCl0.5Br2.5, CsPbBr1.3I1.7 and CsPbBr2I1) placed above the BaFCl:Eu/Gd (Fig. 5b). Upon X-ray irradiation, each region displayed distinct PersL colors corresponding to their respective emitters. As Eu2+ PersL decayed over time, the emission from the QDs faded sequentially: yellow (~10 s), followed by red (~60 s). After 120 s, the Sm2+ PersL became invisible due to its faster decay compared to Eu2+ and Mn2+, while the emission from CsPbCl0.5Br2.5 shifted from blue-green to blue.

Benefiting from its rapid charging capability, the BaFCl:Sm/Gd-integrated transparent PMMA film enables low-dose PersL imaging. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 40, after just 5 s of X-ray irradiation at a dose of 1.6 μGy, a time-delayed X-ray image of the standard Pb line-pair template demonstrates a resolution of up to 20 lp mm−1, as validated by gray-value contrast analysis. Further analysis of the modulation transfer function (MTF) (Fig. 5c) confirms a spatial resolution of ~25.7 lp mm−1 at an MTF value of 0.251. The dose rate (0.32 Gy/s) is an order of magnitude lower than that used in medical diagnostics (5.5 μGy/s)52,53, while the resolution outperforms most previously reported PersL systems (Supplementary Table 2) and conventional flat-panel X-ray detectors (typically lower than 5 lp mm−1)54. Moreover, time-delayed images reveal embedded structures in commercial circuit boards that are otherwise invisible (Fig. 5d), highlighting the potential of this system for ultralow-dose, high-resolution, and background-free radiographic imaging.
paper_content.methods:
Chemicals and reagents
BaF2 (99.9%), BaCl2·2H2O (99.99%), EuCl3·6H2O (99.9%), GdCl3·6H2O (99.99%), SmCl3·6H2O (99.9%), MnCl2·4H2O (99.9%), TbCl3·6H2O (99.99%), CaF2 (99.5%), CaCl2 (99.9%), SrF2 (99.9%), SrCl2·6H2O (99.99%), Cs2CO3 (99.9%), C2H3ClSi (99%), C2H3BrSi (98%), C2H3SiI (97%), Pb(CH3COO)2·3H2O (99.99%), cyclohexane (99.9%), N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF, ≥98%), Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) were all purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Reagent Co. 1-Octadecene (ODE, 90%), Oleic acid (OA, 90%) and Oleylamine (OAm, ≥98%) were supplied by Sigma Aldrich Co. Commercial SrAl2O4:Eu/Dy, CaAl2O4:Eu/Nd, Sr13Al22Si10O66:Eu, ZnS:Cu/Co, and CaS:Eu phosphors were purchased from Shenzhen Looking Long Technology Co. Gd2O2S:Tb was purchased from Felles Photonic Instruments (China) Co. Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) was purchased from Shenzhen Song Shine Technology Co. All chemicals employed in the experiment were of analytical grade and used directly without further treatment.

Synthesis of BaFCl:2Eu/1Gd and other phosphors
BaFCl:2Eu/1Gd was synthesized via a high-temperature solid-state reaction. A stoichiometric mixture of 10 mmol BaF2, 9.4 mmol BaCl2·2H2O, 0.4 mmol EuCl3·6H2O and 0.2 mmol GdCl3·6H2O was thoroughly ground in a mortar for 15 min. The resulting powder was heated at a rate of 7°C/min to 800°C and sintered for 1 h under a flowing 5% H2/N2 atmosphere. After cooling to room temperature, the product was ground for 5 min to yield the BaFCl:2Eu/1Gd phosphor. Other BaFCl-based phosphors, including BaFCl:Eu, BaFCl:Sm/Gd, BaFCl:Mn/Gd, BaFCl:Tb/Gd were synthesized using the same procedure by substituting the corresponding dopant precursors.

Synthesis of flexible BaFCl:Eu/Gd-integrated PDMS film
BaFCl:Eu/Gd phosphor (0.5 g) was dispersed into 1.1 g of PDMS (prepolymer: crosslinker = 10:1 by weight) and stirred for 20 min at room temperature to achieve a homogeneous mixture. The resulting slurry was then cured at 70°C for 2 h, yielding a flexible BaFCl:Eu/Gd-integrated PDMS film.

Synthesis of cesium-oleate (Cs-OA) precursor
Cs2CO3 (0.409 g), ODE (20 mL), and OA (1.25 mL) were added into a 50 mL three-neck flask. The mixture was degassed under N2 at 120°C for 1 h, then heated to 150°C until a clear solution formed. The resulting Cs-oleate solution was transferred to a 10 mL volumetric flask and stored for subsequent use.

Synthesis of CsPbX3 quantum dots (QDs)
Pb(CH3COO)2·3H2O (0.0759 g) was loaded into a 50 mL three-neck flask, followed by the sequential addition of 5 mL ODE, 2.5 mL OA, 2.5 mL OAm, and 250 µL Cs-OA. Then mixture was heated to 110°C under a nitrogen atmosphere and maintained for 45 min. Subsequently, the temperature was rapidly increased to 220°C, at which point 200 µL of a halide precursor solution (Cl, Br, and I in the desired molar ratio) was quickly injected. After 10 s of reaction, the flask was immediately cooled in an ice-water bath to room temperature. The resulting solution was centrifuged at ~5700 × g for 5 min to remove the supernatant. The precipitate was redispersed in 6 mL cyclohexane and centrifuged again at ~4600 × g for 5 min.

Synthesis of composite pattern
BaFCl:Eu/Gd (1 g), BaFCl:Sm/Gd (0.3 g), and BaFCl:Mn/Gd (1 g) phosphors were each dispersed in 1.1 g, 0.33 g, and 1.1 g of PDMS, respectively. The mixtures were then cast into a silicone butterfly mold, with each phosphor occupying designated regions. The mold was then cured at 70°C for 2 h to form the composite pattern. The wings embedded with BaFCl:Eu/Gd phosphor were further decorated with various halide perovskite QDs.

Synthesis of BaFCl:Sm/Gd-integrated film
PMMA powder (0.65 g) was dissolved in 3 mL of DMF by heating to 70°C under stirring for 4 h to obtain a transparent solution. A 1 mL aliquot of this solution was then mixed with 50 mg of BaFCl:Sm/Gd and stirred for 2 h until homogeneous. The resulting mixture was ultrasonicated for 5 min, poured into a glass mold, and left to stand for 10 min to eliminate air bubbles. Finally, the film was cured at 70°C for 2 h to obtain the BaFCl:Sm/Gd-integrated film.

Characterizations
X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was collected using a powder diffractometer (Bruker D8 Advance) equipped with a Cu-Kα radiation (λ=1.5405 Å). Microstructure images and elemental compositions was obtained using a scanning electron microscope (SEM) (Japan Hitachi SU8010) equipped with an energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS, Aztec X-Max 80T). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analyzes were performed using Thermo Fisher Scientific K-Alpha with a tube voltage of 15 kV and a tube current of 10 mA. Photoluminescence (PL) and photoluminescence excitation (PLE), and photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) were carried out using Edinburgh FS-5 spectrofluorometer (Xenon Lamp, 150 W). X-ray excited optical luminescence (XEOL) spectra, X-ray excited persistent luminescence (PersL) spectra, and PersL decay curves were recorded using a spectrometer (OmniFluo 960 X-ray, Zolix, China) coupled with an X-ray tube and Hamamatsu CR131 Photomultiplier Tube. The afterglow curves reported in this work represent photon counts directly obtained from the spectrometer. The PersL spectra presented in Fig. 4a–c, Supplementary Figs. 8a, 22, 31, 34, 35a, b, and 38 were recorded using a fiber-coupled spectrometer (QEpro) linked to the X-ray source, with an acquisition time of ~5 s. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) was performed using an Agilent 7700 instrument. Thermoluminescence (TL) curve was tested by LTTL-3DS type TL 3D spectrometer. Raman microscope (Gloucestershire, UK) was utilized to acquire Raman spectra. The temperature-dependent XEOL spectra were recorded by TAIZI Godzilla fiber spectrometer (Shanghai, China) with a copper heater. Atomic-resolution integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) and high-resolution TEM images were conducted using a Double spherical aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope (Spectra 300, Thermofisher, US). UV-vis spectra were measured using a Craic Technologies micro-spectrophotometer. Pulsed X-ray excited decay curve was measured using an X-ray excitation luminescence lifetime test system (picoX 5084, Shanghai UPU Optoelectronic Technology co.). X-ray imaging experiments were conducted using a custom-built setup including a miniature X-ray tube and an ORCA-Fusion BT camera (C15440-20UP).

Measurement of PersL luminescence brightness: 100 mg of phosphor powder was evenly spread on a transparent plate and gently pressed with a glass plate to ensure uniform thickness. The prepared sample plate was then placed on the probe of a photometer (Xinbao Instrument, SM218E). The sample was irradiated with X-rays at 50 kV for 1 min, and the initial afterglow luminance was recorded immediately after the X-ray source was turned off.

First-principles DFT calculations were carried out using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP, version 5.4.4) with the projector augmented wave (PAW) method55. The exchange–correlation functional was treated within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) using the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional56. A plane-wave cutoff energy of 400 eV was employed. Geometry optimizations were performed until the residual forces on all atoms were less than 0.03 eV Å⁻¹. Brillouin-zone integrations were performed using a 3×3×3 Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh for a 4×4×2 supercell. The self-consistent electronic convergence criterion was set to 10−4 eV. The defect formation energies (Ef) of three types of F− defects, F− located inside the Gd cluster, on the surface of the Gd cluster, and far from the Gd cluster, were calculated according to the following equation:
Ef = Edefect − Eperfect (1)
Where Eperfect and Edefect represent the total energies of the Gd-doped supercell without and with F− Frenkel defects, respectively. To elucidate the formation energy and migration tendency of F− Frenkel defects, the F− ions were systematically displaced from their original lattice sites by -0.2 Å, -0.4 Å, -0.6 Å, -0.8 Å, -1.0 Å, -1.5 Å, 0.2 Å, 0.4 Å, 0.6 Å, 0.8 Å, 1.0 Å, and 1.5 Å, respectively.

Gd L-edge XANES simulations were performed using the finite difference method for near-edge structure (FDMNES) code (version 2025.5.5), a DFT-based and fully relativistic program for ab initio X-ray spectroscopy calculations57,58. To identify the formation of Gd-rich clusters in BaFCl, structural models containing different amounts of Gd3+ ions were constructed and relaxed using DFT optimization to minimize manual bias prior to FDMNES simulations. Preliminary calculations of the Gd L2,3-edge were carried out in the multiple scattering mode (Green’s formalism) under the muffin-tin approximation using the energy-dependent Hedin–Lundqvist exchange potential to rapidly identify the structural configurations consistent with the experimental spectra. Subsequently, accurate simulations were conducted using the finite difference method with a self-consistent field cluster radius of 6 Å. The cluster radius (R) was progressively increased until spectral convergence was achieved, and in this case, R = 6.5 Å was found to be sufficient. To ensure optimal agreement with experimental results, convolution parameters were further refined by comparing the simulated and measured spectra.

Energy migration from traps to Gd3+ activators was modeled using Monte Carlo simulations (version 3.12.4)30,59. Specifically, the spatial distribution of traps and activators was constructed based on the EXAFS-derived structural model (Fig. S17a). In the clustered configuration, the actual Gd3+ doping concentration was set to 2%, and the lattice parameters of BaFCl were taken as a=b=4.418 Å, c=7.281 Å, and α=β=90°. A total of 40 clusters were generated, each modeled as a 1 nm-diameter sphere with Gd3+ ions randomly distributed inside, and randomly positioned within a 10 nm cubic crystal. Trap states were also randomly distributed within the clusters. To compare the differences in energy transfer between clustered and uniform configurations, a non-clustered model was constructed in which both traps and Gd3+ ions were randomly distributed throughout a 10 nm cubic crystal, while maintaining identical structural and compositional parameters. A Förster energy transfer framework with a Förster radius of ~1 nm was employed to describe the charge transfer dynamics between traps and Gd3+ activators. Each Monte Carlo simulation was repeated 1000 times to ensure statistically reliable results.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, Yang and coworkers employ a host-guest doping strategy, utilizing Gd³⁺-mediated cluster traps within the
BaFCl lattice to achieve violet persistent luminescence (PersL). These platforms can efficiently transfer energy to activators
like Eu2+, Sm2+, Tb3+, and Mn2+, enabling tunable multicolor PersL under X-ray irradiation. The application of EXAFS in
conjunction with DFT to characterize trap states demonstrates a certain degree of innovation. Nevertheless, some problems
still need to be addressed.
1. It seems that Fig. S15b is not well-fitted. Is it necessary to refit it and conduct an analysis?
2. From TL analysis (Fig. S17 a), it seems that the mechanistic explanations for the PersL within the two models, which may
involve both shallow and deep trap states. you cannot selectively analyze only the TL spectra within the range of 300-400K
(Fig. 3 e, Fig. S17 b-c). Furthermore, is there a phenomenon of trap-state electron tunneling that leads to long afterglow?
3. The carriers trapped in deep traps can be gradually transferred to the activator (Eu2+, Sm2+, Tb3+, and Mn2+) through
tunneling-mediated energy transfer, which constitutes a critical mechanism underlying energy transfer processes, and the
authors should explicitly clarify this point (RSC Advances, 2015, 5, 82704-82710)
4. From Figs. 4g–l, the sole introduction of Eu²⁺, Sm²⁺, Tb³⁺, and Mn²⁺ dopants can also lead to the formation of new trap
states for PersL. Combining the trap states generated by Gd3+, it is crucial to consider whether the observed long afterglow
phenomenon originates from the migration of charge carriers among these trap states, rather than being exclusively
attributed to energy transfer mechanisms. The PersL mechanism still needs to be further elaborated.
5. The existing systems are already very complex. Without a clear mechanism, why did the author choose to further conduct
experiments with using perovskite materials? Does the author want to illustrate something more meaningful? Moreover,
lead-based perovskites also have instability and toxic issues.
6. The spatial resolution is approximately 25.7 lp/mm, whereas the corresponding dose rate on the same material is only
0.32 μGyair/s. Why does one performance indicator show a significantly higher value, whereas the other remains relatively
low? What factors contribute to this discrepancy?
7. "BaFCl:1Gd and BaFCl:2Eu/1Gd"—a consistent and precise notation style should be employed to explicitly reflect the
compositional ratios, as determined by ICP-OES analysis, instead of utilizing a vague or generalized format.
8. The fabrication of PersL materials and widely used doping strategy for light-emitting applications are hot topics in
chemistry and materials. To arouse a broad interest from readership in this field, some strongly related works on the recent
fabrications of PersL materials (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 5281; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202502782; CCS
Chemistry, 2023, 5, 2866), and the wide doping strategy for light-emitting applications (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 9491;
Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202505322; Chem. Soc. Rev. 2021, 50, 5564) could be included as references.
9. As an excitation source, the X-ray irradiation dose must be explicitly stated in all figure captions; otherwise, it may lead to
the misconception that a high quantum yield was achieved using a large radiation dose.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This work reports a new strategy for developing multicolor X-ray–excited
persistent luminescence (PersL) materials, which can be further extended to design
highly efficient PersL systems and enable multifunctional optical applications. By
constructing Gd3+-mediated cluster traps within alkaline-earth fluorochloride hosts to
minimize energy loss during electron migration, the authors achieve efficient emission
across the violet, yellow, and red spectral regions. Notably, bright PersL is realized
within a single, robust, and scalable host, thereby minimizing compatibility issues and
simplifying integration into multifunctional optical devices. In particular, the X-ray–
excited PersL achieved through cluster construction is remarkably efficient.
BaFCl:Gd/Eu exhibits an integrated PersL intensity 3.5 times higher than that of the
benchmark green-emitting SrAl₂O₄:Eu/Dy. The initial luminance of ≈4.53 cd m⁻² is
exceptionally high for a violet PersL material. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate
the use of these PersL materials as excitation sources for perovskite quantum dots to
achieve full-color time-domain dynamic displays, as well as for low-dose, high-
resolution delayed X-ray imaging.
Owing to the scalable preparation method, high performance, and excellent air
stability, these materials show clear potential for commercialization. Overall, this is a
highly valuable contribution and suitable for publication. I recommend acceptance after
the authors address the following points to strengthen the manuscript.
1. XPS spectra indicate the coexistence of Eu2+ and Eu3+ in the as-prepared
BaFCl:Eu, whereas only PersL from Eu3+ was observed. Why was no PersL from Eu3+
detected? In addition, efficient Gd3+ → Eu3+ energy transfer is commonly reported, yet
no Eu3+ PersL is observed in the BaFCl:Gd/Eu system. Could the authors clarify this
phenomenon?
2. Both the X-ray tube voltage and current influence the PersL intensity. The
authors reported that “Elevating the X-ray tube voltage from 10 to 50 KV resulted in
an additional 65.8-fold enhancement in PersL intensity...”. Was the X-ray tube current
kept fixed? If so, please provide the detailed value.
3. The photograph in Figure 2i lacks a scale bar, which should be included for clarity.
4. When comparing PersL intensity, the authors used SrAl O :Eu/Dy as a reference,
2 4
whereas for luminance comparison, CaAl O :Eu/Nd was used. Why not use the same
2 4
reference material for consistency? As shown in Figure 2f, the PersL intensities of
SrAl O :Eu/Dy and CaAl O :Eu/Nd appear similar.
2 4 2 4
5. The authors state that efficient emission was achieved across the violet, yellow,
and red spectral regions. However, only the PLQY values of BaFCl:Eu/Gd and
BaFCl:Sm/Gd are provided. I suggest that the PLQY of BaFCl:Eu/Mn should also be
included for completeness.
6. The authors attribute the full-color PersL to radiative energy transfer from
BaFCl:Eu/Gd PersL to the QDs via reabsorption. It would strengthen the claim to

7. CsPbX quantum dots have been widely investigated for X-ray detection and

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This review report regards the manuscript “Ultrabright Multicolor X-ray Persistent Luminescence Enabled by Gd-mediated
Trap Clusters” submitted to Nature Communications. The manuscript presents an investigation into the use of Gd as a
bridging element to connect charge-trapping centers in BaFCl to luminescent centers. The central idea - that introducing Gd
creates clusters of defects and luminescent centers which can universally enhance persistent luminescence - is interesting
and of potential importance to the field. Finally BaFCl:Eu/Gd is combined with perovskite quantum dots to obtain persistent
luminescence over a wide range of colors and the materials is also tested for X-ray imaging applications.
However, despite the promise of the concept, the manuscript suffers from several critical shortcomings in execution and
presentation. The work lacks focus, the conclusions are not consistently supported by experimental data, and there is a lack
of clarity in the methodology used to evaluate luminescence intensities which raises doubts about the reported intensities
(one of the more interesting results of the manuscript). These concerns raise doubts about the reliability of the results and
prevent me from recommending publication in its current form. Below I grouped the most important concerns per theme.
Concerns regarding the proposed mechanism:
1. Throughout the manuscript there is an ambiguity regarding the processes of charge transfer and energy transfer. There is
no clear distinction between the part of the process driven by charge transfer (trapping and detrapping) and the part related
to energy transfer (between Gd3+ ions and from Gd3+ to the activator). It is unclear what the recombination center in this
material is.
2. It is proposed that Frenkel defects play an important role in the persistent luminescence mechanism. For this the authors
refer to references 7 and 33. In reference 7 the involvement of Frenkel defects is implied based on DFT calculations but
notably no Frenkel defects are observed in EPR. Similar conclusions can be drawn from reference 33, so the statement is
not supported by any experimental evidence.
3. The mechanism proposed in Figure S22 implies the simultaneous detrapping of both electron and holes and subsequent
recombination at Gd3+. Based on results from numerous other persistent phosphor, it is highly improbable that this takes
place at the same temperature.
4. Monte Carlo simulations are included in the manuscript but they are not coupled to any of the experimental results. The
only conclusion that follows from the ‘simulation’ is that the energy transfer is more probable is the donor and acceptor are
closer together which is a well known experimental observation.
Experimental details:
There is a lot of information in the supplementary but key information is missing.
1. How were persistent luminescence intensities in cd/m² obtained? Given that the intensity of persistent luminescence is
one of the ‘selling points’ of the manuscript this information is important.
2. What was the excitation intensity or wavelength during quantum yield measurements? The quantum yield of persistent
phosphors is known to be intensity dependent so this is important information.
3. How were DFT calculations performed? DFT is used a lot throughout the manuscript but very little information about the
calculations or the results is available. Instead only the interpretation of the results is included in the manuscript.
4. The stability of several materials in ‘air’ is recorded over 60 days ‘under repeated irradiation at one-day intervals’.
SrAl2O4 is stable in air so presumably the decrease in intensity is due to radiation damage but there is no way to tell due to
the lack of details in the manuscript.
Quantification of persistent luminescence intensities and comparison to benchmarks:
1. The results of persistent luminescence intensities are scattered over several figures but none of the figures have tics or
numbers on the y-axis so it is impossible to compare intensities. I would have liked to see the afterglow and TL of the
Eu, Gd, Eu/Gd and Eu/Lu sample in one figure with comparable intensities.
2. To quantify the performance of the BaFCl:Eu/Gd the material’s persistent luminescence is compared to other persistent
luminescent materials such as SrAl2O4:Eu,Dy, CaAl2O4:Eu,Nd, … However, the comparison is flawed because these
materials, benchmarks for UV/VIS excited persistent luminescence, contain much lighter elements so the X-ray attenuation
will be lower. The initial intensity for commercial SrAl2O4:Eu,Dy powder after excitation with UV light is in the order of 10
cd/m² which is higher than the intensity reported here for BaFCl:Eu/Gd.
3. The quantum yield is reported under UV excitation and the values obtained for SrAl2O4:Eu,Dy and BaFCl:Eu/Gd are
compared to each other. This is not a fair comparison as SrAl2O4:Eu,Dy exhibits trapping and detrapping under UV
excitation while BaFCl:Eu/Gd does not.
4. For some of the BaFCl compositions the initial intensities (but not the decay curves) are reported in cd/m², a photometric
unit taking into account the eye sensitivity. However, the emission of BaFCl:Eu,Gd is almost entirely (>80%) located under
400 nm where the eye sensitivity is zero (< 0.01). This raises a question as to how this can give rise to such a high intensity
of 4.53 cd/m². Especially considering that SrAl2O4:Eu,Dy which has an emission that almost perfectly coincides with
maximum eye sensitivity (~1) has an emission intensity of at most 10 cd/m² and is only 5 times weaker than the
BaFCl:Eu/Gd phosphor (according to 2f).
5. Afterglow times up to 168 hours are reported but this is highly dependent on the sensitivity of the equipment used to
record the persistent luminescence. It is standard practice to report the time needed to reach a certain threshold intensity or
at least report the intensity of the light after the stated persistent luminescence time (and the integration time used after
168h).
6. In the conclusions it is stressed that the Sm2+ intensity is increased by a factor 150.3. However, in Figure 5 the red
luminescence isn’t visible anymore after 120 seconds. This raises more questions about how the results are presented in
the manuscript.
7. The material is combined with quantum dots to obtain persistent luminescence over the entire spectrum. But the spectra
are normalized so there is no information about how intense the luminescence of the quantum dots is in the end. Also, how
efficient is the light from the persistent luminescence of BaFCl:Eu/Gd converted to visible quantum dot emission?

Previous studies have shown that shallow traps with depths around 0.69 eV are
optimal for room-temperature PersL emission, whereas deeper traps (>0.9 eV) mainly
contribute to photostimulated luminescence under optical excitation [Adv. Mater.
2020, 32, 2003881; Chem. Sci. 2019, 10, 5452–5460; Matter 2023, 6, 4261–4273].
Liu et al. further demonstrated that short-range displacements of fluoride ions
generate transient shallow traps, while long-range displacements form long-lived deep
traps. Electrons in shallow traps can spontaneously escape to the conduction band
over time, accompanied by defect self-healing, whereas electrons in deep traps require
external optical or thermal stimulation to migrate to luminescent centers (Nature 2021,
590, 410–415).
Therefore, we selectively analyzed the TL spectra within the 300–400 K range to
highlight the contribution of shallow traps that dominate PersL behavior at room
temperature. According to the reviewer’s helpful comment, Fig. S20 has been revised

with Eu-doped BaFCl, and the corresponding trap depth increases from 0.9 eV to 0.95
eV, indicating that the bright PersL observed at room temperature is predominantly
governed by shallow traps rather than deep ones.”

20493]. This t-1 decay behavior has since been widely recognized as a characteristic

1974, 9, 4497; Nat. Mater. 2012, 11, 58; J. Alloys Compd. 2010, 504, 177]. Following
these precedents, we analyzed the PersL decay profiles of BaFCl:Eu, BaFCl:Eu/Gd,

Response 4: Thanks for the reviewer’s kind comment. Liu et al. (Nature 2021, 590,
410–415) reported that “through elastic collisions between high-momentum X-ray
photons and light fluoride ions, anion Frenkel defects are generated within the crystal
lattice, which can trap thermalized low-energy electrons and enable long-lived photon
storage. Specifically, fluoride vacancies and interstitials act as electron and hole traps,
respectively. Displacements of fluoride ions over short and long distances lead to the
formation of transient shallow and long-lived deep trap states, respectively.” In this
context, the introduction of different activators does not alter the intrinsic nature of
these traps but instead modulates their depths and distributions. As shown in Fig. S18,
the deep-trap population is markedly reduced in Gd/Eu co-doped BaFCl compared
with Eu-doped BaFCl, while the corresponding trap depth increases from 0.90 eV
(450/500) to 0.952 eV (476/500). In contrast, the shallow trap depth remains nearly
unchanged, but its thermoluminescence (TL) intensity is significantly enhanced. The
reduction in deep-trap population upon Gd incorporation indicates a decreased
electron-trapping efficiency, suggesting that charge migration from deep to shallow
traps is not promoted in Gd/Eu co-doped BaFCl.

Gd3+ to Eu2+, Sm2+, Tb3+, and Mn2+ have been extensively reported in previous studies

Comment 5: The existing systems are already very complex. Without a clear
mechanism, why did the author choose to further conduct experiments with using

Response 5: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment. The
experiments involving perovskite quantum dots (QDs) were not intended to further
complicate the PersL mechanism but rather to demonstrate the exceptionally bright
violet afterglow of the Gd/Eu-codoped BaFCl system, which is sufficiently intense to
excite perovskite QDs. This experiment serves as an application-oriented
proof-of-concept, independent of the underlying PersL mechanism.
Because purely inorganic afterglow systems often face challenges in achieving
fine spectral tunability, we employed perovskite QDs as a color-tunable model system.
Their well-defined emission bands and high compatibility with violet excitation
enabled the realization of bright, full-spectrum afterglow modulation through simple
7
physical mixing of Gd/Eu:BaFCl and perovskite QDs. We can reasonably speculate
that, with appropriate heterostructure design and interface engineering, both the color
and brightness of the afterglow emission could be further optimized.
We fully acknowledge that lead-based perovskites suffer from toxicity and
stability issues. In future studies, such QDs can be replaced with environmentally
benign alternatives—such as organic fluorophores or carbon-based dots—which offer
comparable tunability and excitation compatibility. Therefore, the present results can
serve as a guiding framework for research groups experienced with organic or
inorganic carbon dots to further develop this concept.
Finally, the observed color-tunable afterglow also implies the potential for
multi-color, time-resolved delayed X-ray imaging. However, realizing this prospect
will require a dedicated time-gated imaging setup and extensive additional
experiments, which are beyond the scope of the present study.
Comment 6: The spatial resolution is approximately 25.7 lp/mm, whereas the
corresponding dose rate on the same material is only 0.32 μGyair/s. Why does one
performance indicator show a significantly higher value, whereas the other remains
relatively low? What factors contribute to this discrepancy?
Response 6: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In X-ray imaging,
image quality is primarily governed by the scintillation brightness and the
signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the detected photons. Under higher radiation doses, a
larger number of X-ray photons interact with the scintillator, generating stronger light
output and consequently improving image contrast and spatial resolution. Therefore,
conventional X-ray imaging typically requires relatively high radiation doses to obtain
clear and detailed images, which inevitably raises concerns regarding radiation safety.
Enhancing the performance of X-ray detection materials is thus crucial for achieving
high-quality imaging under reduced exposure conditions.
In this work, we employ X-ray–excited persistent luminescent (PersL) materials
to enable time-delayed X-ray imaging, where the emitted afterglow contributes to
image formation even after the cessation of X-ray excitation. Theoretically, the
8
resolution of delayed images increases with higher radiation doses, as stronger
excitation produces brighter afterglow emission. As shown in Fig. R4, the image
resolution indeed improves with increasing X-ray dose rate from 0.23 to 3.64 μGy
(Adv. Funct. Mater. 2024, 34, 2409156). However, our objective is to balance image
quality with radiation safety by maintaining high spatial resolution under low-dose
conditions. Based on both literature reports and our experimental results, the
Gd/Eu-codoped BaFCl system exhibits remarkably high spatial resolution (~25.7
lp·mm-1) even at a low dose rate of only 0.32 μGy·s-1. This exceptional performance
originates from its intense PersL emission, which preserves image contrast and
effectively compensates for the reduced excitation intensity. Therefore, the high
spatial resolution achieved under low radiation dose does not imply any inconsistency
but rather highlights the superior photon utilization efficiency of the developed
X-ray–excited persistent luminescent material, enabling high-clarity imaging even
under minimal irradiation.

that no Eu3+ emission was observed because hole–Eu3+ centers could not form in
Eu3+-doped fluoride compounds, as supported by electronic structure calculations
(Nature, 2021, 590, 410–415). Similarly, Chen et al. demonstrated that Eu3+ ions,
whose 4f ground states lie within the valence band, are unable to trap holes under
irradiation, thereby preventing electron–hole recombination and persistent
luminescence generation (Matter, 2023, 6, 4261–4273). Therefore, the absence of
Eu3+ PersL in our system is likely due to the inability of Eu3+ ions to effectively
capture trapped holes. In the BaFCl:Gd/Eu system, the excited Eu2+ ions exhibit a
much larger absorption cross-section than Eu3+, which further suppresses the
observation of Eu3+ emission.

Concerns regarding the proposed mechanism:
Comment 1: Throughout the manuscript there is an ambiguity regarding the
processes of charge transfer and energy transfer. There is no clear distinction between
the part of the process driven by charge transfer (trapping and detrapping) and the part
related to energy transfer (between Gd3+ ions and from Gd3+ to the activator). It is

Response 1: We greatly appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. In Figure 1
and its caption, we have now explicitly distinguished between the charge-transfer (CT)
and energy-transfer (ET) processes. Under X-ray irradiation, elastic collisions
between high-momentum X-ray photons and light fluoride ions induce the formation
of anion Frenkel defects within the crystal lattice, thereby enabling long-lived photon
storage (refs: Mod. Probl. Condens. Matter Sci. 1986, 13, 473–525; Laser Photonics
Rev., 2025, 2500092; Nature, 2021, 590, 410–415; Comment 2). These defects
generate fluoride vacancies and interstitials that act as electron traps and hole traps,
respectively. The trapped charge carriers can subsequently migrate toward
luminescence centers, where radiative recombination occurs. In the absence of Gd3+
codoping, mainly the CT process occurs—electrons are captured from the conduction
band and later released to recombine with holes at luminescence centers, resulting in
weak persistent luminescence (PersL). Upon Gd3+ codoping, the detrapping process
primarily occurs within Gd3+-rich clusters, where released electrons migrate toward
Gd3+ ions and recombine with localized holes, thereby populating the excited states of
Gd3+. This is subsequently followed by an ET process from Gd3+ to the activator ions,
which markedly enhances the PersL intensity.
Considering that the primary distinction between the samples with and without
Gd3+ lies in the detrapping and subsequent energy-transfer processes, the
electron-trapping step from the conduction band was omitted from the schematic for
clarity, but is illustrated in Fig. S24.
illustration of structural evolution in MFCl (M = Ca, Sr, Ba) upon Gd3+ doping and
the corresponding charge transfer (CT) and energy transfer (ET) pathways. For clarity,
Cl- ions are omitted from the crystal structures. Two Gd3+ ions substitute for three
Ba2+ ions, generating one Ba2+ vacancy to maintain charge neutrality. The Gd3+
dopants tend to aggregate within the crystal lattice, promoting the formation of
X-ray-induced Frenkel defects in Gd-rich clusters. Upon Gd3+ codoping, the
detrapping process predominantly occurs within these clusters, where released
electrons migrate toward Gd3+ ions and recombine with captured holes, populating the
excited states of Gd3+. Subsequently, ET from Gd3+ to the activator ions gives rise to
strong multicolor PersL. In contrast, the absence of such clusters leads to long-range
carrier migration and increased non-radiative losses, yielding faint PersL.
Based on the above analysis, we propose that upon Gd3+ codoping, the radiative
recombination centers are predominantly located at Gd3+ ions within Gd-rich clusters,
as most X-ray-induced Frenkel defects are largely confined to these regions. In
contrast, in the absence of Gd3+ codoping, recombination mainly occurs at the
luminescence centers (Nature, 2021, 590, 410–415). When electron detrapping takes
place within the clusters, carrier migration distances are minimized, thereby reducing
nonradiative losses. Without such confinement, however, carriers undergo long-range
migration accompanied by substantial energy dissipation. Consequently, the formation
16
of Gd-rich clusters markedly enhances the persistent luminescence performance.
To more clearly distinguish the charge-transfer processes (trapping and

activators), as well as to clarify the recombination centers, we have redrawn Fig. S24
and added the corresponding discussion (see Comment 3).
Comment 2: It is proposed that Frenkel defects play an important role in the
persistent luminescence mechanism. For this the authors refer to references 7 and 33.
In reference 7 the involvement of Frenkel defects is implied based on DFT

Response 2: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment. The formation of
Frenkel defects under X-ray irradiation is physically reasonable and has been widely
reported in previous studies (Point defects in materials, Wiley, New York, 1988;
Defects and defect processes in nonmetallic solids Wiley, New York, 1985; Laser
Photonics Rev., 2025, 2500092; Low Temperature Physics, 2018, 44, 269–277; Mod.
Probl. Condens. Matter Sci., 1986, 13, 473–525; J. Phys. Chem. Solids, 1960, 17,
88–92). Although direct observation of X-ray-induced Frenkel defects remains
challenging—mainly due to the lack of in-situ techniques compatible with
high-energy X-rays and associated radiation safety concerns—numerous works have
employed EPR and optical methods to provide indirect yet compelling evidence of
their presence.
Upon X-ray irradiation, energetic photons interact with the crystal lattice,
transferring sufficient energy to displace ions from their equilibrium positions. This
process generates Frenkel defects, consisting of a vacancy and an interstitial ion pair.
In fluoride-based hosts, the anion sublattice (F⁻) is particularly susceptible to such
displacements due to its relatively low binding energy. The formation of Frenkel
defects introduces additional charge carriers within the bandgap, thereby altering the
electrical transport behavior. Consequently, the electrical conductivity measurement
17
serves as an effective probe to confirm defect generation. The increase in conductivity
after X-ray exposure arises from the elevated concentration of mobile charge carriers
(such as F⁻ vacancies or interstitials). By comparing the conductivity before and after
irradiation, one can quantitatively infer the formation and evolution of
radiation-induced Frenkel defects in the lattice. From this view of point, we conducted
the electrical conductivity measurement for the BaFCl:Eu/Gd.

Response 3: We greatly appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment highlighting
that the simultaneous detrapping of both electrons and holes is highly improbable. We
apologize for the misleading depiction in the previous version of the figure. Under
X-ray irradiation, elastic collisions between high-momentum X-ray photons and light
fluoride ions generate anion Frenkel defects within the crystal lattice. These defects
create fluoride vacancies and interstitials, which serve as electron and hole traps,
respectively (refs: Mod. Probl. Condens. Matter Sci. 1986, 13, 473–525; Laser
Photonics Rev., 2025, 2500092; Nature, 2021, 590, 410–415; Comment 2). Upon
Gd3+ codoping, these traps are predominantly confined within Gd-rich clusters.
Electrons in shallow traps can be thermally released over time and migrate toward
19
luminescence centers. Separately, trapped holes may also migrate to these centers;
however, these two detrapping events occur at different temperatures rather than
simultaneously. During recombination, the radiative energy released from these
charge carriers populates the excited states of Gd3+ ions, which subsequently transfer
energy to the activator ions. To clarify this sequence, we have redrawn Figure S24 and
provided revised mechanistic explanations in the manuscript.

During the XEOL process, X-ray photons primarily interact with heavy atoms
through the photoelectric effect, producing hot electrons and deep holes. Subsequent
electron–electron scattering and Auger relaxation generate numerous low-energy
secondary carriers. XEOL emission occurs when the excited states of activator ions
are populated through the radiative recombination of these thermalized carriers. In
contrast, during the X-ray-excited PersL process, elastic collisions between
high-momentum X-ray photons and light fluoride ions induce the formation of anion
Frenkel defects, enabling long-lived photon storage. These defects act as electron and
hole traps, and the trapped charge carriers migrate separately to luminescence centers
over time. Upon Gd3+ codoping, the traps become spatially confined within Gd-rich
clusters, promoting efficient radiative recombination through Gd3+ and subsequent
energy transfer to activator ions.

Response 4: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. We first
experimentally confirmed the presence of Gd-rich clusters in BaFCl:Gd/Eu. Since it is
not feasible to prepare two samples with and without Gd clustering while maintaining
identical chemical compositions, we employed Monte Carlo simulations to
complement the experimental observations. These simulations were designed to
elucidate the differences in electron migration from traps to activators between
clustered and uniformly distributed configurations under equivalent compositional
conditions. The direct correlation between the Monte Carlo simulations and our
experimental results lies in the use of the crystal structure model derived from the
EXAFS analysis (Fig. S17a). Considering that the excited-state population of Gd3+
originates from the radiative recombination energy of electrons and holes, we adopted
a Förster energy transfer framework to simulate the charge transfer process between
traps and activators (Nature Nanotechnology, 2021, 16, 1011–1018).
The following methodological details have been added to the revised
Supporting Information for clarity.
Energy migration from traps to Gd3+ activators was modeled using Monte Carlo
simulations[5]. Specifically, the spatial distribution of traps and activators was
constructed based on the EXAFS-derived structural model (Fig. S17a). In the
clustered configuration, the actual Gd3+ doping concentration was set to 2%, and the
lattice parameters of BaFCl were taken as a = b = 4.418 Å, c = 7.281 Å, and α = β =
90°. A total of 40 clusters were generated, each modeled as a 1 nm-diameter sphere
with Gd3+ ions randomly distributed inside, and randomly positioned within a 10 nm
cubic crystal. Trap states were also randomly distributed within the clusters. To
compare the differences in energy transfer between clustered and uniform
configurations, a non-clustered model was constructed in which both traps and Gd3+
ions were randomly distributed throughout a 10 nm cubic crystal, while maintaining
21
identical structural and compositional parameters. A Förster energy transfer
framework with a Förster radius of approximately 1 nm was employed to describe the
charge transfer dynamics between traps and Gd3+ activators.[6,7] Each Monte Carlo
simulation was repeated 1000 times to ensure statistically reliable results.

First-principles DFT calculations were carried out using the Vienna Ab initio

The exchange–correlation functional was treated within the generalized gradient

k-point mesh for a 4 × 4 × 2 supercell. The self-consistent electronic convergence
criterion was set to 10-4 eV. The defect formation energies (E) of three types of F-

Subsequently, accurate simulations were conducted using the finite difference method

progressively increased until spectral convergence was achieved, and in this case, R =

Comment 3: Throughout the manuscript but also in the responses to questions raised
by other reviewers a comparison is made between the TL peaks at low and high
temperatures. Was the data corrected for thermal quenching? Without a proper
correction it is impossible to draw meaningful conclusions from the comparison of TL
intensities at different temperatures.
Response 3: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. The
temperature-dependent PersL spectra mentioned were not included in the current
manuscript but were provided in the previous response letter to address the
mechanism-related question raised by Reviewer 1. In that response, the PersL spectra
of the BaFCl:Gd phosphor were measured after X-ray irradiation at temperatures
ranging from 89 K to 249 K to qualitatively illustrate the thermally assisted PersL
process. Although the data were not corrected for thermal quenching, we believe that
the comparative analysis remains meaningful for the following reasons. First, the
PersL spectra were mainly used, together with the fitting of PersL intensity as a
function of t-1, to illustrate the possible PersL process. This analysis was not directly
related to the quantitative comparison of absolute PersL intensities, and the approach
has been accepted by Reviewer 1. Second, thermal quenching of inorganic phosphors
generally becomes more significant at elevated temperatures. However, in our
measurements, the PersL intensity increased as the temperature rose from 89 K to 249
K. Therefore, even if the data were corrected for thermal quenching, the observed
trend—an increase in PersL intensity with temperature—would remain unchanged.
Consequently, the qualitative interpretation and conclusions drawn from these results
remain valid.
Comment 4: The new version of Figure S24 and the accompanying text now suggest
that either holes or electrons are trapped on Gd3+, which would imply the creation of
the proposed model is not plausible.
Response 4: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment. The
migration of trapped holes or electrons to lanthanide activators has indeed been
discussed in several previous studies. For instance, it has been reported that “Electrons
in shallow traps can spontaneously escape over time to the conduction band with a
concurrent defect self-healing process, whereas electrons in deep traps require extra
energy in the form of either optical or thermal stimulation to migrate to Tb3+ emitters.
Trapped holes can also migrate towards Tb3+ emitters, forming hole–Tb3+ centres that
radiatively recombine with captured electrons” (Nature, 2021, 590, 410–415).
Similarly, Light: Science & Applications (2022, 11, 51) reported that “The trivalent
lanthanides are expected to attract an electron (or hole) first and then will draw a hole
(or electron) due to the Coulomb force. In all cases, the trivalent lanthanides
eventually bind the excitons as this is the origin of energy. The excitons recombine
and transfer the energy to the trivalent lanthanides that bind the excitons. The trivalent
lanthanides are excited from the ground state to the excited state, which is followed
by the non-radiative relaxation processes and final emitting of PersL.” These studies
indicate that the capture of electrons or holes by lanthanide ions does not necessarily
lead to the formation of divalent or tetravalent species (e.g., Gd2+ or Gd4+). Based on
this understanding, we have further clarified the related discussion in the revised
Supporting Information.
During the XEOL process, incident X-ray photons predominantly interact with
heavy atoms via the photoelectric effect, generating hot electrons and deep holes.[8,9]
Subsequent electron-electron scattering and Auger relaxation processes produce
numerous low-energy secondary carriers. XEOL emission arises when these
thermalized carriers recombine radiatively, populating the excited states of activator
ions. In contrast, during X-ray-excited PersL, elastic collisions between
high-momentum X-ray photons and light fluoride ions induce the formation of anion
Frenkel defects, which serve as long-lived traps for electrons and holes. The trapped
carriers migrate separately to luminescent centers and recombine over time. Trivalent
5
lanthanides can sequentially attract an electron (or hole) and subsequently capture the
opposite charge through Coulomb interaction, leading to exciton formation. The
recombination of these excitons transfers energy to the lanthanide ions, generating
PersL emission. Upon Gd3+ codoping, the traps become spatially confined within
Gd-rich clusters, which enhances radiative recombination through Gd3+ and facilitates
efficient energy transfer to the activator ions.
Comment 5: The authors have added conductivity measurements as a proof of the
existence of Frenkel defects but the analysis is lacking. Under X-ray irradiation a lot
of free charge carriers are created (and this is also voltage dependent). How can you
discriminate between the contribution of these free charge carriers and those of
mobile species like F interstitials?
Response 5: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment. X-ray
photons interact with the lattice atoms primarily through the photoelectric and
Compton scattering effects, generating hot electrons and deep holes. Subsequent
electron–electron scattering and Auger relaxation processes produce a large number of
secondary electrons, resulting in abundant charge carriers with lower kinetic energies.
These carriers rapidly thermalize through phonon interactions and accumulate near
the conduction and valence bands within a subpicosecond timescale. Their transport
toward luminescence centers typically occurs within 10-12–10-8 s (ref: ACS Energy
Lett., 2021, 6, 739–768). Consequently, the current signal arising purely from these
free charge carriers should appear and vanish almost instantaneously upon switching
the X-ray on or off, as also demonstrated in Adv. Mater., 2019, 31, 1901644
(“Flexible, Printable Soft-X-Ray Detectors Based on All-Inorganic Perovskite
Quantum Dots”). As this figure cannot be used directly, it is not included here.
In contrast, as shown in our current–time measurements (Fig. S18),
BaFCl:Eu/Gd exhibits a gradual current rise more than 7s after the X-ray is switched
on, and decays slowly with a delay exceeding 7 s after the X-ray is turned off. This
delayed response cannot be accounted for by free charge carriers and is instead
consistent with the behavior of mobile species such as F- interstitials. We therefore
6
attribute this slow component to the migration of mobile charged defects, specifically
anion Frenkel defects induced under irradiation. Based on theoretical calculations,
similar diffusion-controlled relaxation of F interstitials has been reported in fluoride
materials (Nature, 2021, 590, 410–415), where interstitial F- ions gradually migrate
back to their original vacancy sites. These observations reveal that the measured
conductivity predominantly arises from defect-mediated ionic transport, providing
strong evidence for the formation of Frenkel defects under X-ray irradiation.
The following contents have been added in the revised manuscript and
supporting information.
As shown in Figure S18, the current gradually increases upon X-ray irradiation
and decays slowly with a delay exceeding 7 s after the X-ray is turned off, while the
peak current rises at higher tube voltages. These observations indicate that the
measured conductivity predominantly arises from defect-related ionic transport under
X-ray irradiation.

Concerns with regard to the proposed mechanism.

ranging from 89 K to 249 K to qualitatively illustrate the thermally assisted PersL

the comparative analysis remains meaningful for the following reasons. First, the
PersL spectra were mainly used, together with the fitting of PersL intensity as a
function of t-1, to illustrate the possible PersL process. This analysis was not directly
related to the quantitative comparison of absolute PersL intensities, and the approach
has been accepted by Reviewer 1. Second, thermal quenching of inorganic phosphors
generally becomes more significant at elevated temperatures. However, in our

Response 4: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment. The
migration of trapped holes or electrons to lanthanide activators has indeed been
discussed in several previous studies. For instance, it has been reported that “Electrons
in shallow traps can spontaneously escape over time to the conduction band with a
concurrent defect self-healing process, whereas electrons in deep traps require extra
energy in the form of either optical or thermal stimulation to migrate to Tb3+ emitters.
Trapped holes can also migrate towards Tb3+ emitters, forming hole–Tb3+ centres that
radiatively recombine with captured electrons” (Nature, 2021, 590, 410–415).
Similarly, Light: Science & Applications (2022, 11, 51) reported that “The trivalent
lanthanides are expected to attract an electron (or hole) first and then will draw a hole
(or electron) due to the Coulomb force. In all cases, the trivalent lanthanides
eventually bind the excitons as this is the origin of energy. The excitons recombine
and transfer the energy to the trivalent lanthanides that bind the excitons. The trivalent
lanthanides are excited from the ground state to the excited state, which is followed
by the non-radiative relaxation processes and final emitting of PersL.” These studies

lead to the formation of divalent or tetravalent species (e.g., Gd2+ or Gd4+). Based on
this understanding, we have further clarified the related discussion in the revised
Supporting Information.
During the XEOL process, incident X-ray photons predominantly interact with
heavy atoms via the photoelectric effect, generating hot electrons and deep holes.[8,9]
Subsequent electron-electron scattering and Auger relaxation processes produce
numerous low-energy secondary carriers. XEOL emission arises when these
thermalized carriers recombine radiatively, populating the excited states of activator
ions. In contrast, during X-ray-excited PersL, elastic collisions between
high-momentum X-ray photons and light fluoride ions induce the formation of anion
Frenkel defects, which serve as long-lived traps for electrons and holes. The trapped
carriers migrate separately to luminescent centers and recombine over time. Trivalent
5
lanthanides can sequentially attract an electron (or hole) and subsequently capture the
opposite charge through Coulomb interaction, leading to exciton formation. The
recombination of these excitons transfers energy to the lanthanide ions, generating
PersL emission. Upon Gd3+ codoping, the traps become spatially confined within
Gd-rich clusters, which enhances radiative recombination through Gd3+ and facilitates
efficient energy transfer to the activator ions.
Comment 5: The authors have added conductivity measurements as a proof of the
existence of Frenkel defects but the analysis is lacking. Under X-ray irradiation a lot
of free charge carriers are created (and this is also voltage dependent). How can you

Response 5: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment. X-ray
photons interact with the lattice atoms primarily through the photoelectric and
Compton scattering effects, generating hot electrons and deep holes. Subsequent
electron–electron scattering and Auger relaxation processes produce a large number of
secondary electrons, resulting in abundant charge carriers with lower kinetic energies.
These carriers rapidly thermalize through phonon interactions and accumulate near
the conduction and valence bands within a subpicosecond timescale. Their transport
toward luminescence centers typically occurs within 10-12–10-8 s (ref: ACS Energy
Lett., 2021, 6, 739–768). Consequently, the current signal arising purely from these
free charge carriers should appear and vanish almost instantaneously upon switching
the X-ray on or off, as also demonstrated in Adv. Mater., 2019, 31, 1901644
(“Flexible, Printable Soft-X-Ray Detectors Based on All-Inorganic Perovskite
Quantum Dots”). As this figure cannot be used directly, it is not included here.
In contrast, as shown in our current–time measurements (Fig. S18),
BaFCl:Eu/Gd exhibits a gradual current rise more than 7s after the X-ray is switched
on, and decays slowly with a delay exceeding 7 s after the X-ray is turned off. This
delayed response cannot be accounted for by free charge carriers and is instead
consistent with the behavior of mobile species such as F- interstitials. We therefore
6
attribute this slow component to the migration of mobile charged defects, specifically
anion Frenkel defects induced under irradiation. Based on theoretical calculations,
similar diffusion-controlled relaxation of F interstitials has been reported in fluoride

back to their original vacancy sites. These observations reveal that the measured
conductivity predominantly arises from defect-mediated ionic transport, providing
strong evidence for the formation of Frenkel defects under X-ray irradiation.
